meta.name: YAP! Diagnostic Wizard — Yap-Wizard (Branching Spec) v2
meta.description: Full branching questionnaire v2. All branches now have 10-12 steps. Each END node contains collected_data ready to map to Flask /api/generate payload keys: category, problem, tech_stack, experimental_detail.
meta.changelog: v2: Branch B deepened from 7 to 12 steps (added auth, rate limiting/caching, background workers, containerization). Branch C deepened from 7 to 12 steps (added vector DB, model deployment, prediction storage, serving infrastructure). Branch D deepened from 6 to 11 steps (added power management, frontend dashboard, data retention, OTA updates). Branch E deepened from 5 to 11 steps (added real-time API reactivity, performance optimization, interactivity model, deployment/sharing, and statement layer).

S1.question: Alright. Your README is a blank void and your LinkedIn says 'passionate developer'. What cursed thing did you actually build?

options.label: 🌐  A web app — it runs in a browser and judges people
⚙️  Backend / API / CLI — no UI, just raw terminal energy
📊  Data, ML, or AI — you trained something and now it has opinions
🔩  Hardware / IoT — there are wires on your desk and you're not sure why
🎨  Creative / Generative — vibes over function, art over tickets

A1.question: Who is this web app actually FOR? And don't say 'everyone', that's not a target audience, that's a lack of planning.

options.label: 👤  Individual users — solo productivity, personal tools, or 'I built this for myself'
🏢  Businesses or teams — dashboards, SaaS, internal tools your manager will take credit for
🔧  Other developers — dev tools, CLI wrappers, libraries, stuff only 0.1% of people understand
🎮  Entertainment or community — games, social features, 'engagement metrics'

A2.question: What's the CORE thing users actually DO in your app? If your app was a verb, what would it be?

options.label: 📝  Create & manage stuff — CRUD, forms, dashboards, the bread and butter
🔍  Search, filter, and discover — users finding needles in haystacks
🤖  Automate or AI-generate — something happens without the user lifting a finger
🤝  Connect & collaborate — multiple users doing things together in real-time or async
📊  Visualize & track — charts, metrics, 'data-driven insights' for the stakeholders

A3.question: Does your app have USER ACCOUNTS — login, registration, sessions, the whole authentication circus?

options.label: ✅  Yes — full auth. Users log in, have profiles, own their data
🔑  Yes but I outsourced it — OAuth only (Google, GitHub, etc.), not my problem
❌  No auth — it's public, open, or single-user. No passwords were harmed.

A4.question: Does your app talk to a DATABASE? Something persistent where data lives between sessions?

options.label: ✅  Yes — a proper database. Data persists and I lose sleep over migrations
🔥  Yes — but it's BaaS: Firebase, Supabase, PocketBase. I let them deal with it.
❌  No DB — stateless, local storage, or everything lives in the user's browser

A5.phase: BRANCH A — Web App — Tech Stack
A5.question: Alright, what FRONTEND framework are you using? Please say something interesting.

options.label: ⚛️  React — the default choice of people who stopped questioning defaults
▲  Next.js — React but with SSR, routing, and an identity crisis about being a framework
💚  Vue / Nuxt — the sensible choice that nobody hypes but everyone enjoys
🔥  Svelte / SvelteKit — you compiled your opinions away and it felt good
🌐  Vanilla JS / HTML / CSS — no framework, no bundler, no therapy
🅰️  Angular — you work at a corporation and TypeScript is your love language

A6_react.question: React detected. What's powering the backend / server side?

options.label: 🟢  Node.js + Express — the classic combo, circa 2015, still running in prod
⚡  Node.js + Fastify / Hono — Express but you've read the benchmarks
🐍  Python + Flask / FastAPI — polyglot energy, frontend in JS, backend in Python
🔥  Firebase / Supabase — there is no backend, only vibes and cloud functions

A6_next.question: Next.js — respectable. Are you using it full-stack or just as a frontend with a separate API?

options.label: 🏗️  Full-stack — API routes or Route Handlers live inside the Next.js app itself
🔀  Separate backend — Next.js is just the frontend, API lives elsewhere
☁️  Serverless — Vercel / Netlify edge functions, no persistent server

A6_vue.question: Vue / Nuxt — good taste. What's the backend situation?

options.label: 🟢  Node.js + Express / Fastify — keeping it in the JS family
🐍  Python + Django / FastAPI — mixing languages like a true professional
🐘  PHP + Laravel — you're not afraid of .php files and we respect that
🔥  Supabase / Firebase — the backend is someone else's problem

A6_svelte.question: Svelte / SvelteKit — you love compile-time. How are you handling the backend?

options.label: 🏗️  SvelteKit full-stack — form actions, server routes, the whole deal
🟢  Separate Node.js / Express backend
🔥  BaaS — Firebase, Supabase, Pocketbase

A6_vanilla.question: No framework — I respect the commitment. What's generating or serving the HTML?

options.label: 📄  Pure static files — HTML, CSS, JS. Deployed to a CDN or GitHub Pages
🟢  Node.js backend serving templates (Express + EJS/Handlebars)
🐍  Python backend (Flask / FastAPI + Jinja2 templates)

A6_angular.question: Angular. A bold, enterprise-flavored choice. What's the backend?

options.label: ☕  Java + Spring Boot — the full enterprise combo. Your PM is proud.
🟢  Node.js + NestJS — TypeScript on both sides, you are built different
🐍  Python + Django REST Framework
🔷  .NET / C# — Microsoft ecosystem, all the way down

A6_nostack.question: No database, got it. What frontend framework are we working with?

options.label: ⚛️  React / Next.js
💚  Vue / Nuxt
🔥  Svelte / SvelteKit
🌐  Vanilla JS — browser APIs are all I need

A7_sql.question: Database time. What flavor of data storage are you inflicting on yourself?

options.label: 🐘  PostgreSQL — the adult choice. ACID-compliant and you know what that means.
🍃  MongoDB — schemaless because you haven't decided what you're building yet
🔴  MySQL / MariaDB — classic, reliable, your hosting provider defaulted to it
⚡  Redis — caching layer, session store, or you're using it as a primary DB (bold)
🪶  SQLite — runs on file, perfect for local dev or 'I shipped to prod with this'

A7b_orm.question: Are you talking to that database like a civilized developer or writing raw SQL at 2am?

options.label: 🔷  Prisma — type-safe, schema-first, and your IDE autocompletes your queries
🌊  Drizzle — Prisma but you read the bundle size discourse
🐍  SQLAlchemy / Tortoise ORM — Python ORM, because you're living in two worlds
🌱  Sequelize / TypeORM — the OGs of Node.js ORMs, been here since forever
📜  Raw SQL — you write JOIN statements by hand and feel nothing

A8_deployment.question: Where does this app actually LIVE when it's not on localhost?

options.label: ▲  Vercel — one push to main and it's live, the way God intended
🟠  Netlify — like Vercel but you got here first
🐳  Docker + VPS (DigitalOcean / Hetzner / Linode) — self-hosted, full control
☁️  AWS / GCP / Azure — enterprise cloud, expense reports required
🏠  Localhost only — it works on my machine and that's enough for now
🚂  Railway / Render / Fly.io — the developer-friendly middle ground

A9_problem.question: Final boss. What PROBLEM did this app exist to solve? Before your app, what was the annoying reality?

options.label: 🗂️  Everything was scattered — too many tabs, tools, or spreadsheets managing one thing

collects.problem: Consolidates scattered workflows and tools into a single unified interface

options.label: ⏱️  A repetitive manual task was eating hours — it screamed for automation

collects.problem: Automates a repetitive, time-consuming manual process

options.label: 😵  The existing solution was ugly, overcomplicated, or paywalled

collects.problem: Provides a simpler, faster, or more accessible alternative to existing solutions

options.label: 🕳️  This solution didn't exist — I had the idea and committed the crime

collects.problem: Fills a genuine gap — no existing tool solved this specific problem

options.label: 🧪  It's a learning project — the problem I solved was my own ignorance

collects.problem: Built as a learning project to explore and master a specific technology or concept

A_END.message: Stack locked. README incoming. You may have used a framework to avoid thinking, but at least you're honest about it.
A_END.payload_note: Aggregate all collects from this path into category, problem, tech_stack, and experimental_detail keys.

B1.question: Backend dev spotted. What specific kind of server-side abomination did you create?

options.label: 🔌  A REST API — endpoints, status codes, and someone will definitely misuse the 200 OK
🔷  A GraphQL API — you prefer querying with a query language inside a query
🖥️  A CLI tool — runs in terminal, has --help, makes devs feel powerful
🤖  A bot or automation script — does things on a schedule while you sleep
🔗  A microservice — one specific job, deployed in a container, part of a bigger system
📦  A library or SDK — other developers are your users, god help them

B2.question: What is this API / service actually responsible for? Its raison d'être, if you will (it's fancier in French).

options.label: 🚦  Core data layer — handles all business logic and database ops for a frontend app

collects.problem: Serves as the core data and business logic layer for a client application

options.label: 🔄  Integration glue — connects 2+ external APIs or services so they play nice

collects.problem: Acts as an integration layer, connecting and normalizing multiple third-party services

options.label: ⚡  Performance offload — handles CPU or I/O heavy work so the main app doesn't choke

collects.problem: Offloads computationally intensive tasks to improve overall system performance

options.label: 🛡️  Auth / security gateway — handles tokens, permissions, rate limiting, the bouncer

collects.problem: Centralizes authentication, authorization, and API security concerns

options.label: 📬  Event / queue processor — consumes messages from a queue and does things with them

collects.problem: Processes asynchronous events and messages from a queue system

B2_cli.question: A CLI tool — nice. What problem does running this command actually solve?

options.label: 🏗️  Project scaffolding / boilerplate generator — creates files so you don't have to

collects.problem: Scaffolds projects or generates boilerplate code to accelerate developer workflows

options.label: 🔁  Automates a repeated dev workflow — build, deploy, lint, test pipeline helper

collects.problem: Automates a repetitive developer workflow or CI/CD step

options.label: 🔍  Data processing or file manipulation — reads, transforms, outputs structured data

collects.problem: Processes, transforms, or analyzes data files directly from the command line

options.label: 🌐  Hits an API and formats the output — a nice wrapper around something annoying

collects.problem: Provides a clean terminal interface for interacting with an external API

B2_bot.question: A bot. Nice. Where does this bot actually live and operate?

options.label: 💬  Discord / Slack / Telegram — it lives in a chat platform and people talk to it

collects.problem: Operates as a chat bot within a messaging platform (Discord / Slack / Telegram)
collects.experimental_detail: Chat Bot Integration

options.label: 🌐  Web scraper / crawler — reads websites and extracts data like a digital vacuum

collects.problem: Scrapes and extracts structured data from web pages automatically
collects.experimental_detail: Web Scraping Bot

options.label: ⏰  Scheduled job / cron worker — runs silently at set intervals without anyone watching

collects.problem: Runs scheduled background tasks and automations at defined intervals
collects.experimental_detail: Scheduled Automation Worker

options.label: 📧  Email / notification automation — sends the right thing to the right person at the right time

collects.problem: Automates email or notification delivery based on triggers or schedules
collects.experimental_detail: Notification Automation System

B2_lib.question: A library — so other developers are your users. What problem does your package solve for them?

options.label: 🎨  UI components — a reusable component library so people stop reinventing buttons

collects.problem: Provides a reusable library of UI components for consistent interface development

options.label: 🛠️  Utility functions — helpers, formatters, validators that every project needs

collects.problem: Provides a collection of reusable utility functions to simplify common programming tasks

options.label: 🔌  API client / SDK wrapper — makes integrating a specific service less painful

collects.problem: Wraps a complex API or service in a clean, developer-friendly SDK

options.label: 🧩  Framework plugin / middleware — extends an existing framework with new capabilities

collects.problem: Extends a framework or tool with additional capabilities via a plugin or middleware

B3_lang.question: What language is this backend written in? Don't be ashamed. We've seen worse.

options.label: 🟢  Node.js — JavaScript everywhere, consequences everywhere
🐍  Python — readable, powerful, and the data science crowd refuses to leave
🦫  Go — compiled, fast, minimal, and you've explained goroutines at least once this week
🦀  Rust — memory safe, blazingly fast, and you have a crab emoji somewhere in your bio
☕  Java / Kotlin — enterprise grade, Spring flavored, 500mb JAR included
🐘  PHP — yes, still. It runs half the internet and it will outlive us all.

B4_node.question: Node.js backend. What framework, if any, did you slap on top of it?

options.label: 🚂  Express.js — the jQuery of backend frameworks. Ubiquitous for a reason.
⚡  Fastify — Express but you care about microseconds and write schema upfront
🐦  NestJS — Angular for the backend, decorators everywhere, OOP maximalist
🔥  Hono — edge-first, tiny, and you benchmarked it against everything else
📦  No framework — raw Node.js http module, you are a different kind of person

B4_python.question: Python backend. Which framework did you choose to express your pain?

options.label: 🌶️  Flask — minimal, micro, and you wrote the auth yourself (god help us)
⚡  FastAPI — async, typed, auto-docs. The correct answer for new projects.
🎸  Django — batteries included, ORM included, opinions very much included
🎯  Django REST Framework — Django but you're building an API, not rendering templates

B4_go.question: Go. Bold. Did you use a router/framework or are you net/http-ing like a true Gopher?

options.label: 🌿  Gin — fast HTTP framework, good defaults, most people's first Go web choice
🌊  Echo — similar to Gin but with slightly different opinions about middleware
🔥  Fiber — Express-inspired Go framework, familiar feel, fast runtime
🔩  Raw net/http — no external dependencies, just you and the standard library

B4_rust.question: Rust backend. You clearly enjoy fighting the borrow checker. Which framework?

options.label: 🪓  Axum — Tokio-native, ergonomic, the current community favorite
🚀  Actix-web — blazingly fast, actor model, benchmarks love it
🌊  Warp — filter-based, composable, functional programming vibes

B4_java.question: Java / Kotlin. Enterprise tier. What's the framework?

options.label: 🌱  Spring Boot — the industry standard, XML config nightmares included at no extra charge
⚡  Quarkus — cloud-native, fast startup, Kubernetes-first Java
🔷  Ktor (Kotlin) — async, lightweight, and you chose Kotlin for a reason
🔴  Laravel — the PHP framework that made PHP developers feel good about their life choices
⚡  Symfony — enterprise PHP, component-based, used by Laravel under the hood anyway
🕰️  Vanilla PHP — no framework, just include files and regrets

B5_db.question: Does this backend need to PERSIST data somewhere — a database, cache, or storage service?

options.label: 🐘  PostgreSQL — you've heard 'just use Postgres' enough times to finally listen
🍃  MongoDB — document model, flexible schema, you'll normalize it later (you won't)
⚡  Redis — cache, session store, pub/sub, or bravely your primary DB
🔴  MySQL / MariaDB — the classic, reliable, your tutorial used it in 2018
📁  No database — stateless service, reads from files, or delegates storage elsewhere

B6_auth.question: Does your API authenticate callers? And how — because 'I'll add auth later' is not an answer that ages well.

options.label: 🔑  API Keys — simple, stateless, the classic 'header: Bearer your-secret-shame'
🎫  JWT / OAuth 2.0 — tokens, scopes, refresh flows, the full auth ceremony
🔐  Third-party auth provider — Auth0, Clerk, Firebase Auth, Cognito. Someone else's problem.

collects.auth_strategy: Third-Party Auth Provider (Auth0 / Clerk / Firebase Auth)

options.label: 🔒  Session-based — server-side sessions, cookies, your grandma's auth system (still works)
🏝️  No auth — public API, internal only, or you live dangerously

B7_ratelimit.question: Does your service have any RATE LIMITING or CACHING strategy? Or do you just pray your server survives traffic?

options.label: 🚦  Rate limiting implemented — token bucket, sliding window, or API gateway level (NGINX, Kong)

collects.tech_stack: Rate Limiting (Token Bucket / Sliding Window / API Gateway)
collects.experimental_detail: API rate limiting enforced at middleware or gateway level

options.label: ⚡  Redis caching — hot data cached in Redis, TTL configured, cache invalidation nightmares included

collects.experimental_detail: Redis used as an in-memory caching layer to reduce DB load

options.label: 🌐  CDN / edge caching — static assets and responses cached at the network level (Cloudflare, Fastly)

collects.experimental_detail: CDN-level caching for static and semi-static API responses

options.label: 📦  In-memory / app-level cache — LRU cache, memoization, or a dictionary that got out of hand

collects.experimental_detail: Application-level in-memory cache for frequently computed results

options.label: 🙏  None — it either doesn't need it, or you're just optimistic about traffic

collects.tech_stack: No Caching / Rate Limiting (Stateless or Low-Traffic Service)

B8_workers.question: Does your service run any BACKGROUND JOBS or ASYNC WORKERS — things that chug away while the main thread pretends everything is fine?

options.label: 🔁  Celery / RQ / BullMQ — task queue with workers, retries, and a dashboard you'll check once

collects.experimental_detail: Asynchronous task processing with a dedicated worker queue system

options.label: ⏰  Cron jobs / scheduled tasks — runs at set intervals, crontab or APScheduler, silent and judgemental

collects.experimental_detail: Time-based job scheduling for periodic background processing

options.label: 📡  Message queue / event-driven — Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS. It consumes events and reacts.

collects.tech_stack: Message Queue / Event-Driven Workers (Kafka / RabbitMQ / SQS)
collects.experimental_detail: Event-driven architecture with message broker for async worker communication

options.label: 🌊  Async/await only — Python asyncio or Node.js event loop, no separate worker process

collects.tech_stack: Async I/O (asyncio / Node.js Event Loop, no separate workers)
collects.experimental_detail: Concurrency handled via async event loop without separate worker processes

options.label: 🧘  No background workers — it's synchronous, request-response, and that's fine

B9_containerize.question: Is this service containerized? Does it live in a Docker image, or does it run directly on the machine like it's 2012?

options.label: 🐳  Docker — Dockerfile written, image built, 'it works on my machine' is no longer an excuse

collects.experimental_detail: Service packaged as a Docker image for consistent, reproducible deployment

options.label: 🏗️  Docker Compose — multi-container setup, app + DB + Redis all in one docker-compose.yml symphony

collects.experimental_detail: Multi-service Docker Compose setup orchestrating app, database, and cache containers

options.label: ☸️  Kubernetes / Helm — you have replicas, health checks, and an ops team that hates you

collects.experimental_detail: Production-grade container orchestration with Kubernetes for scaling and reliability

options.label: 📦  Deployed directly — systemd service, PM2, or bare metal. The container discourse bores you.

collects.experimental_detail: Process-managed deployment without containerization

B10_observability.question: How do you know when this thing breaks? Do you have monitoring, or does a user DM you on Discord?

options.label: 📊  Prometheus + Grafana — metrics scraped, dashboards configured, you feel like an SRE

collects.experimental_detail: Full observability stack with Prometheus metrics scraping and Grafana dashboards

options.label: 🔍  Structured logging — JSON logs to stdout, shipped to ELK / Loki / Datadog for analysis

collects.experimental_detail: Structured JSON logging pipeline for centralized log aggregation and search

options.label: 🐛  Sentry / error tracking — catches exceptions, sends alerts, screenshot of your shame in the inbox

collects.experimental_detail: Real-time error tracking and alerting via Sentry or equivalent

options.label: 📝  Basic console logs — console.log or print() all the way down, no shame (okay, some shame)
🙈  Nothing — production is a black box and you're not ready to open it

B11_deploy.question: Final question. Where does this backend actually RUN in production — or at least, where does it pretend to?

options.label: ☁️  Cloud function / serverless — scales to zero, costs pennies, cold starts haunt your dreams
🖥️  VPS / dedicated server — you SSH in and it runs as a systemd process, old school respect
🚂  PaaS — Railway, Render, Fly.io. Push code, get URL, check dashboard, pay invoice.
☸️  Kubernetes cluster — EKS, GKE, AKS, or self-hosted. You have a runbook.
🏠  Localhost only — it works on my machine and the README will say 'deployment: coming soon'

B_END.message: Backend fully interrogated — auth, caching, workers, monitoring, the works. Your README will make your endpoints sound intentional and your architecture look like it was planned from day one.
B_END.payload_note: Aggregate all collects into category, problem, tech_stack, and experimental_detail keys.

C1.question: Data / ML / AI spotted. What kind of model crime are we documenting here?

options.label: 🤖  Classical ML — scikit-learn, XGBoost, random forests, things that fit in memory
🧠  Deep learning — PyTorch, TensorFlow, GPUs, and electricity bills
🦜  LLM / GenAI — you're prompting, fine-tuning, or RAG-ing something large
📊  Data analysis / visualization — pandas, charts, insights, not a model but still science
🔁  Data pipeline / ETL — ingests, transforms, loads. The plumbing of data.

C2_classical.question: Classical ML. What domain is your model pretending to understand?

options.label: 📈  Regression — predicts a number, like house prices or your project's due date
🏷️  Classification — predicts a category. Spam or not spam. The eternal problem.
🔍  Clustering — unsupervised, finds hidden groups, no labels needed or available
🚨  Anomaly detection — spots the weird outlier in a sea of normal
💬  NLP with classical ML — TF-IDF, Naive Bayes, text without the transformer drama

C3_classical.question: What data are you feeding this model? What's the input source?

options.label: 📊  Tabular / structured data — CSVs, spreadsheets, SQL exports, the bread and butter
📝  Text data — reviews, articles, comments, logs, anything humans typed
⏰  Time-series — sensor readings, stock prices, anything with a timestamp

C4_stack_classical.question: Tech stack for classical ML. What libraries are actually in your requirements.txt?

options.label: 🔬  scikit-learn — the standard library for ML. If it's not here, are you even ML?
🌲  XGBoost / LightGBM / CatBoost — gradient boosted trees, Kaggle's weapon of choice
📊  statsmodels — you care about p-values and confidence intervals, a true statistician

C2_dl.question: Deep learning. What kind of data is your network trying to make sense of?

options.label: 👁️  Computer Vision — images, video, object detection, segmentation, that kind of fun
📝  NLP / Text — transformers, embeddings, sequence models, understanding language
🎵  Audio / Speech — waveforms, spectrograms, voice, music
🎮  Reinforcement learning — an agent, an environment, a reward function, and a lot of compute

C3_dl_cv.question: Computer Vision. What is the model actually DOING with the images?

options.label: 🏷️  Image classification — label this image. Cat or not cat.
📦  Object detection — find and box every object in the scene
🎭  Segmentation — pixel-perfect region labeling, every pixel gets a class
✨  Image generation / style transfer — creates or transforms images

C3_dl_nlp.question: NLP deep learning. What's the transformer doing?

options.label: 😊  Sentiment analysis / text classification — labeling opinions or categories
✍️  Text generation — generates new text, completions, creative writing
🔍  Information extraction — pulls entities, relationships, facts from text
🌐  Translation / summarization — converts text from one form to another

C3_dl_audio.question: Audio ML. What specifically is the model doing with the sound?

options.label: 🎤  Speech-to-text / ASR — converts spoken words to readable text
🎵  Music generation or classification — creates or categorizes audio
🔊  Sound event detection — identifies events in ambient audio (alarm, cough, etc.)

C4_stack_dl.question: Deep learning framework — the one you actually ran the training loop in?

options.label: 🔥  PyTorch — dynamic graph, research-first, most papers implement in this
🧪  TensorFlow / Keras — static graph, production-first, tf.function hell included
🤗  HuggingFace Transformers — you used a pre-trained model and added a head, valid approach
🔢  JAX / Flax — you need XLA compilation and your loss function has custom gradients

C2_llm.question: LLM / GenAI project. What flavor of LLM work is this?

options.label: 🔗  RAG system — Retrieval-Augmented Generation, your LLM has a knowledge base

collects.problem: Builds a RAG system to give an LLM accurate, grounded, up-to-date knowledge from a custom document corpus

options.label: 🤖  AI Agent — tool-calling, autonomous task execution, it makes decisions

collects.problem: Implements an AI agent capable of using tools and autonomously completing multi-step tasks

options.label: 🔧  Fine-tuned model — you took a base model and trained it on your own data

collects.problem: Fine-tunes a pre-trained language model on domain-specific data for specialized task performance

options.label: 💬  LLM-powered app / chatbot — a product built on top of an API (OpenAI, Gemini, Claude)

collects.problem: Builds a user-facing application or chatbot powered by a large language model API

C3_llm_rag.question: RAG system. What's the document corpus it's grounded in?

options.label: 📚  PDFs / docs — internal knowledge base, company documents, research papers
🌐  Web content / crawled pages — it indexes and queries scraped web data
💾  Database / structured data — queries a SQL or vector DB to ground responses
📝  Codebase — it RAGs over source code for a coding assistant use case

C3b_vector_db.question: Your RAG needs somewhere to store embeddings. What Vector Database are you using to stash those high-dimensional vibes?

options.label: 🌲  Pinecone — fully managed, fast, and you paid for the convenience (fair)

collects.experimental_detail: Pinecone used as the managed vector store for embedding similarity search in RAG pipeline

options.label: 🎨  Chroma — open-source, runs locally or self-hosted, the developer's first vector DB

collects.experimental_detail: ChromaDB used for local/self-hosted vector embedding storage and retrieval

options.label: 🌀  Milvus / Weaviate / Qdrant — open-source but production-grade, you deployed a vector DB cluster

collects.experimental_detail: Production-grade open-source vector database cluster for large-scale embedding retrieval

options.label: 🐘  pgvector — vector search inside PostgreSQL, because why add another service

collects.experimental_detail: Vector similarity search implemented directly inside PostgreSQL via the pgvector extension

options.label: 🔢  In-memory / FAISS — Facebook's similarity search library, no persistent DB, fast and raw

collects.experimental_detail: FAISS used for high-performance in-memory approximate nearest neighbor search

C3_llm_agent.question: AI Agent. What tools can it actually use to get things done?

options.label: 🌐  Web search / browsing — it Googles things and reads pages autonomously
💻  Code execution — it writes and runs code to solve problems
🔌  External APIs — it calls real services (calendar, email, databases, etc.)
🧩  Custom function tools — domain-specific tools you defined for it

C3_llm_ft.question: Fine-tuning. What technique did you use to actually update the weights?

options.label: 🔧  LoRA / QLoRA — parameter-efficient, the sensible choice for consumer hardware
